turns.content: My closest friend from college called last night. His father needs a procedure — real thing, I've known uncle for years — and he asked me for eighty thousand, "just for two months." Here's the thing I didn't say: in 2019 I gave him fifty thousand. Neither of us has mentioned it since. Not once, not him, not me.

That's a heavy one. The fact that the fifty grand from 2019 has never come up once makes this new ask feel different, doesn't it? Like there's already an unresolved chapter sitting between you two.

How are you feeling about it, just between us? Are you leaning toward saying something about the old money, or are you more stuck on whether to lend again at all?

Meanwhile I'm eleven months into saving for a flat down payment. And my wife doesn't know about the 2019 money — it was before the wedding and it just... never came up, and now it's a thing I've apparently decided not to tell her, which I hate. If I move eighty thousand she will definitely notice.

That's a lot of weight on this decision. The old loan sitting there unmentioned, the secrecy with your wife, and now this potentially derailing your down-payment savings... it all feels tangled together.

How are you sitting with the fact that you'd have to hide or explain another big sum to her? Does that part feel heavier than the money itself right now?

I was thinking I'll tell him my money is parked in FDs and mutual funds, all locked in, nothing liquid. It's a small lie and it saves the friendship — he keeps his respect, I keep my savings, nobody has to say the real sentence. Is that wrong? It feels smart and it also feels a bit sick.

It's not the worst instinct in the world — you're trying to protect your savings and your wife's trust without blowing up the friendship. But the fact that it already feels "a bit sick" to you is probably worth listening to. That little voice is usually flagging that the lie isn't just about protecting money; it's about avoiding the real conversation you two still haven't had about the first 50k.

Would it feel different if the lie was just to him, or does the bigger knot come from knowing your wife would still be in the dark either way?

The part that actually keeps me up: someday he'll be standing in my flat at the housewarming, hugging me, and some part of me will still be doing 2019's math. I don't want to become that person — the friend with a ledger in his chest. But I also can't keep being the guy whose money is everyone's buffer.

That image — him at your housewarming, and that quiet arithmetic still running in your head — says a lot. You don't want to carry the score, but you also don't want to keep paying the bill for a friendship that never settles its own debts.

The tricky part is that avoiding the conversation now (with the small lie) might actually lock that ledger in place even tighter, because the 2019 money stays buried and unaddressed. Sometimes the only way to stop keeping mental tabs is to finally put the real number on the table, even if it feels messy.

You don't have to decide tonight, but which part feels more unbearable right now: the risk of him seeing you as unhelpful, or the risk of you quietly resenting him for years?
